content:
Ever since Adobe introduced generative AI features in 2023, I've been using these capabilities in Photoshop to remove unwanted objects and extend photos. For me, the results have been hit or miss, but they're definitely much faster than traditional masking, cloning, and manual smudging methods. However, with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved the "Clean Up" tool and introduced a new "Extend" tool, so I'm curious how Apple's offering compares to Adobe's. So, with the help of a friend, I tested the two tools with different photos to see how they performed.

In this article, my friend Jürg generously provided several photos he took while traveling in Switzerland and around Europe. He's a far better photographer than I am, and his subjects are also far more interesting than what I see in my corner of Ohio. You can see more of his photography on Instagram. I selected six photos from his collection: three to test object removal and three to test image extension.

All photos were taken with an iPhone 17 Pro Max and edited on an iPhone 18 Pro Max running iOS 27.0. The iOS 27 "Clean Up" tool offers three options: Auto, Quick, and High Quality. I kept the setting on "Auto" for all tests.

Photoshop testing was performed on a MacBook Pro running Adobe Photoshop 27.10.0 with the "Firefly Fill & Expand" model. I used the "Object Selection Tool" or "Lasso Tool" to select the object, then chose "Generative Fill" and left the prompt field blank.

For the "Extend" tool, I used the photo's preset extension method. The "Extend" tool in Photos limits how much you can expand the edges of an image, while Photoshop has no such restrictions. To make the comparison as consistent as possible, I used Apple's Photos result as the reference and then asked Photoshop to generate content at a similar size.

I've done my best to make the HDR appearance of photos edited in iOS 27 Photos consistent with those edited in Photoshop, but there are still slight differences.

Making objects disappear

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up tool

First up is removing the red chair in front of the yellow door. This was the first photo I tested with the new "Clean Up" tool, and I have to say, it gave me a very good first impression. The result looks very realistic, and the only real error I noticed is that the rivets behind the left armrest of the chair were also removed instead of being properly reconstructed. However, I don't think most people would notice this, and it wouldn't be hard to clone them back in Photoshop. What really impressed me is that the shadow under the chair was replaced with a texture that matches the surrounding scene and maintains the original lighting.

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop didn't perform as well as Apple's "Clean Up" tool here. The shadow of the chair is still there and looks more like an oil stain. The rivets on the door are in the wrong place, and one is clearly missing. The replacement texture also clearly has more visual flaws. Overall, it's definitely not as clean and realistic as the "Clean Up" tool.

The "Clean Up" tool impressed me here. It not only removed the plate with the bread, but also added reflections of the cups and jars. Notice how it correctly handled the spoon handle in the reflection. A very refined result. The "Clean Up" tool also completely removed the plate's shadow from the napkin. I thought removing a red plate from a red tablecloth of the same color would be a bigger challenge for the "Clean Up" tool, but it had no problem at all! If I had to nitpick, the "Clean Up" tool left some bread crumbs on the plate, but it's easy to just run "Clean Up" again on that area.

Photoshop also managed to remove the plate with the bread well enough, but it similarly had trouble leaving an out-of-place shadow. The napkin looks a bit dirty or wet, but at least Photoshop didn't leave as many annoying crumbs.

This was a much bigger challenge for the "Clean Up" tool. When trying to remove the man on the right, the "Clean Up" tool left a bunch of obvious artifacts. The leaves are too thick. With the white-haired woman standing behind the white flowers on the left side of the photo, the "Clean Up" tool had similar difficulties. The "Clean Up" tool also left a "ghost" of the dog's head, which barely blends into the stone wall but is more obvious in side-by-side comparison.

Photoshop had no trouble removing the woman standing behind the white flowers on the left or the man standing behind the leaves on the right, and realistically filled in both areas. The end result is a very believable photo that looks as if no one was ever there. Photoshop also didn't leave any phantom shadows this time.

Adding content to photos

I thought this photo of an old curved staircase would be a good test because I didn't think either AI would immediately know what they were looking at, so I was curious to see how each would interpret the scene or how they would handle it. The iOS 27 "Extend" tool seems to have interpreted the photo as something more like a ceiling fan, shaping the two ends of the staircase to look like fan blades. Photoshop, on the other hand, simply extended the staircase outward and surprisingly managed to match the wood grain.

The "Extend" tool really lived up to its name here. It extended the scene well and created a very believable final image. Notice how well the windows were repeated. While the bridge on the right could be called too smooth, it still looks fairly believable.

Now let's look at Photoshop's attempt. Honestly, Photoshop, did you even try? By almost any standard, this is a complete failure. Pure, obvious AI slop. The windows and roofline in the upper left corner of the photo look terrible. The bridge on the right doesn't have any of the realistic arches that Apple created, and for some reason Photoshop decided to make the waterfall randomly change direction instead of following the existing river line.

The "Extend" tool once again created a believable image. It's not perfect, but it's clearly much better than Photoshop's result. The "Extend" tool created a believable tabletop with some books or magazines, and the flowers in the vase look more realistic than what Photoshop generated. The decorative pattern above the doorway on the left also surprisingly matches the actual decorations in the photo. There are some oddities on the right side of the photo: the "Extend" tool added a heater, a random wire, and inexplicably added a table.

Perhaps the biggest difference between the "Extend" tool and Photoshop is the ceiling. The "Extend" tool recreated more of the wood from the opposite wall, while Photoshop tried to turn it into something more like a structural beam.

On the other hand, Photoshop seems unable to generate images without obvious AI slop. Its table has too many legs and seems to just "break off" and merge into the floor. The decoration above the doorway is less believable, missing a "swirl" and lacking the textured paint of a real decoration.

I won't say either one is perfect, but when it comes to realism, I think Apple's solution is slightly better than Adobe's.

The good, the bad, and the AI slop

It's worth noting that Photoshop requires a subscription to use, but none of the features I tested consume generative AI credits. Adobe does give users the option to select other AI models that may require credits, but I didn't use those models in my testing. Apple has also indicated that some Apple Intelligence features "may have usage limits" and may charge for expanded use in the future.

It's clear that Apple has made major improvements to the "Clean Up" tool—it's much better than previous iOS versions. I've tried it before and always found it lacking, but now it's really good. The new "Extend" tool is also impressive; I found it clearly superior to Adobe's offering in my testing. Adobe gives you unlimited revisions and the ability to adjust results through prompts, but if extra generations and prompts just keep producing more obvious AI slop, I'd question the value of those benefits. Apple may be more limited in this regard, but their initial results are much better to begin with.

Of course, results will vary depending on the photo, the complexity of the scene, and what you ask the tool to do. The above are just the results I got with the photos I used to test.

What do you think: have you tried Apple's new "Clean Up" and "Extend" tools? If so, what's your take?
